title: State in React - Declarative vs. Imperative Programming
summary: Introduces state as the thing a React UI is derived from, and contrasts declarative (describe the UI per state) with imperative (DOM-manipulating) code using a strike-through to-do example. Ends by showing that a plain variable change does not re-render, which leads to hooks.

concepts.heading: UI as a function of state
points: Core React idea: UI = f(state). The component describes what to show for each value of some data, and the screen follows when that data changes.
Analogy kept short: ice and water are the same thing shown differently depending on a temperature value.
Example app: a to-do item whose text is struck through once done. The state is a boolean isDone, false initially, switched to true when the user clicks the item.

concepts.heading: Declarative version in React
points:
Start with a component rendering

Buy milk

.
Add inline styling through the style attribute, which takes a JavaScript object: style={{ textDecoration: "line-through" }} (outer braces = JSX expression, inner braces = object literal).
Extract the object into a constant, e.g. const strikeThrough = { textDecoration: "line-through" }, so the JSX stays readable.
Make it conditional with a ternary: style={isDone ? strikeThrough : null}. Null means no style applied.
Setting isDone to true in the source shows the struck text, false shows plain text. The code declares how the UI looks under each condition; this is declarative programming.

concepts.heading: Imperative version in plain JavaScript
points: The approach used earlier in the course: fetch the element with document.getElementById and assign to its style.textDecoration property directly.
Add a button with an onClick handler calling a function (strike) that applies line-through, and a second button/function (unStrike) that resets the property.
This is imperative: you explicitly grab an element and tell it what to do at each change. It achieves the same visual result but you must manage every transition by hand.

concepts.heading: Why changing a plain variable is not enough
points: In the declarative component, wiring buttons to functions that set isDone = true / false looks like it should work, but the page does not update.
A component's output is produced when it renders; changing a normal variable afterwards does not trigger React to render again, so the displayed elements stay as they were.

React needs to be told about the change through its own mechanism. Hooks are functions that let a component tie into React state (read it and change it); the next lecture covers the most common one, useState.

(Extra) The entry file renders App once with root.render(<App />). After that React only calls App again (re-renders) when that component's state, its props or a parent changes; a module-level var is none of those, so the click handlers run but the JSX is never re-evaluated.

(Extra) Even if App did re-run, a plain variable declared inside the component would be re-created with its initial value on every render, so it cannot remember anything between renders. State solves both problems.

pitfalls: Expecting a normal variable assignment to refresh the screen; it will not re-render.
Mixing up the two brace pairs in style={{ ... }}.
(Extra) Writing CSS property names with hyphens inside the style object: React expects camelCase (textDecoration, backgroundColor).

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Thinking in state' placed before useState. Blurb: in React the UI is derived from data (UI = f(state)); describe how each state looks instead of issuing DOM commands.

Tasks: (1) render 'Buy milk' with style={isDone ? strikeThrough : null} and flip isDone in code to see both looks; (2) write the imperative version with document.getElementById(...).style.textDecoration and two buttons; (3) wire React buttons to functions that set isDone = true/false, add a console.log, and note that the log runs but the paragraph never changes; (4) explain in one sentence why (no re-render is triggered).
